# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–19 (Complete – Updated 138)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of fifth year** (Chapter 19 opening). Summer 1816 completed with Sir Pitt's death. Spring 1816 events: Rebecca delivers son (Rawdon minor); Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton; moves into Miss Crawley's house; Lady Southdown assumes control; Miss Crawley dies (spring/early summer 1816). **Chapter 18 events (Summer 1816)**: Sir Pitt nearly eighty, afflicted with lumbago; Pitt and Lady Jane visit Queen's Crawley (described as "awful and unfortunate"). Sir Pitt suffers collapse after evening carousing with rum-and-water; dies during summer. **Chapter 18-19 transition**: Pitt becomes Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet, with seat in Parliament and prospect of future honours. Immediately plans to clear estate with ready money. Within three-to-four days of inheriting, changes bearing and fixes plans: will rule justly and honestly, depose Lady Southdown, be friendliest terms with all blood relations. **Chapter 19 (Autumn, fifth year)**: Briggs dismissed by Lady Southdown; Miss Crawley's legacies distributed; Bowls and Firkin receive legacies, marry, set up lodging-house.
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' Coffee-house, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers, Curzon Street May Fair, Fulham, Park Lane, Bond Street, Bayswater, Hyde Park, opera, Knightsbridge, nursery, parlour, ring, Times Office in City), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Faubourg St. Germain, Coldcombe hill farms, Dunholt, Calais, Dunkirk, Red Lion Square, Cursitor Street, Tooting, Gulton, Quenwick, Queen's Crawley, Clapham, Sugar-cane Lodge, Miremere, Valenciennes, Kensington Gardens, Hampshire, Madras, district chapel, tavern, Winchester Cathedral Close, Mudbury, Rectory, Parsonage, Hill farms of Mirecombe, Fuddleston, Southampton Gaol, Dunwick, Crawley Arms, Mudbury (saddler residence), Salwick harbour town, parsonage with lavender.

## Main Characters

**Sir Pitt Crawley (Baronet, elder) – DECEASED (Summer 1816)**
- Nearly eighty; afflicted with lumbago; dislike for respectable society increased with age. **Queen's Crawley visit reception (Chapter 18)**: Initial crude affection; took snuff, leered at Lady Jane, pinched hand; said he shan't be here long; gave Lady Jane valuable pearls (mother's and first Lady Binkie's jewels). **Final evening (Chapter 18)**: In great spirits; narrated Miss Horrocks' singing incident repeatedly; drank extraordinary quantity of rum-and-water with butler Horrocks. **Collapse and death (Chapter 18)**: Suffered sudden collapse at very late hour; conducted to bedroom; brought "back to a sort of life"; could not speak but recognized people. **Final days (Chapter 18)**: Taken out in chair on terrace; Lady Jane favourite; nodded, smiled, uttered inarticulate moans; cried and sobbed when she left. Hester (maid) cruel when unobserved—made faces, clenched fist, screamed insults. After seventy years of cunning, struggling, drinking, scheming, sin and selfishness, became "whimpering old idiot put in and out of bed and cleaned and fed like a baby." **Dies summer 1816**; all blinds pulled down at Hall and Rectory; church bell tolled; chancel hung in black.

**Sir Pitt Crawley (younger) – Now Baronet, MP (Chapter 18-19)**
- **Upon father's death**: Pale face flushes quite red; immediately plans to clear estate with ready money; will not use aunt's legacy previously lest father recover. **Three-to-four days of reign (Chapter 18)**: Bearing changed; plans fixed. Determined to rule justly and honestly, depose Lady Southdown, be friendliest terms with blood relations. Pleased to think he should be chief; proposes to use vast influence for county position to place brother Rawdon and provide decently for cousins; had slight sting of repentance thinking he proprietor of all they hoped for. **Toward Lady Southdown (Chapter 18)**: Called her "Lady Macbeth"; when she waited for sign of weakness or vacillation, rose scared and left library. Pitt told her she won't go away; she let house at Brighton, spent last half-year's dividends; Countess living at inn is ruined woman; he'd waited long for opportunity to take decisive step; impossible two chiefs in family. **Letter to Rawdon (Chapter 18)**: Dictated solemn, elaborate letter with profoundest observations, longest words; filled secretary (Lady Jane) with wonder; she thought of his future oration in House of Commons, his wisdom and genius (fancied him little cold). Letter sent with huge black border and seal to Colonel in London.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 18-19)**
- **Upon receiving Pitt's letter (Chapter 18)**: But half-pleased; thought "What's use of going down to stupid place?"; can't stand being alone with Pitt after dinner; horses there and back will cost twenty pounds. **Wife's ambitions (Chapter 18)**: Rebecca tells him "Of course I mean to go. I mean Lady Jane shall present me at Court next year. I mean your brother shall give you seat in Parliament, you stupid old creature. I mean Lord Steyne shall have your vote and his, and you shall be Irish Secretary, or West Indian Governor, or Treasurer, or Consul, or some such thing."

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley) (Chapter 18-19)**
- **Toward son (Chapter 18)**: When little Rawdon cries from garret, dismisses sardonically; tells Lord Steyne he'll cry himself to sleep; doesn't offer to visit. **Character**: Speedily became vogue among certain class; displays herself at gatherings (fresh pink dress, dazzling white arms, thin hazy scarf, curls, prettiest little foot, finest silk stocking); sings charming French songs, plays piano, charms with wit. **Manipulation of husband (Chapter 18)**: Increases scorn for his paternal tenderness; tells him not to stay home; instructs him to tell Sparks his man that old Sir Pitt is dead and he'll come in for something considerable when affairs arranged; Sparks will tell Raggles (pressing for money), consoling him; begins sipping chocolate. **Toward Briggs (Chapter 19)**: Recognizes fatigued Briggs on street in her dashing little carriage and ponies; pulls up, gives reins to groom, jumps out, holds both Briggs's hands; perfectly good-humoured woman with regard for Briggs; they embrace in passage, retire to Mrs. Bowls's front parlour; Rebecca gives narrative of own life with usual artlessness and candour. **Reminiscence (Chapter 18)**: Tells Miss Briggs "I might have been Silenus's widow. Don't you remember how you peeped in at door and saw old Sir Pitt on his knees to me?" Briggs blushes very much; glad when Lord Steyne ordered her downstairs to make tea.

**Little Rawdon (Son) (Chapter 18-19)**
- **London period (Chapter 18)**: Hidden upstairs in garret or kitchen, scarcely noticed by mother; passed days with French bonne; when Frenchwoman departed, taken to housemaid's bed in garret by compassionate servant. **Relationship with father unchanged**: Rawdon affectionate and devoted; maintains private interviews mornings during shaving; sweetmeats hidden in old epaulet box. Father buys picture-books; walls covered with pictures. Takes accustomed morning walks with father and pony. **Chapter 18 plan**: Rebecca forbids him traveling to Queen's Crawley; instructs Rawdon that boy is too big to travel "bodkin" between them; let him stay in nursery; Briggs can make black frock; tells Rawdon to tell Sparks that old Sir Pitt is dead and son will come in for something considerable.

**Mrs. Bute Crawley – Schemer (Chapter 18)**
- **Character**: Considers herself one of most virtuous women in England. Daughters: Martha paints flowers exquisitely; Emma writes verses in Hampshire Telegraph; Fanny and Matilda sing duets. **Reality**: Nobody sees poor girls drumming at duets in private; Mamma drilling them hour after hour. "Put a good face against fortune and kept up appearances in most virtuous manner." Got over yachting men, parsons, officers; tried to inveigle barristers. **Relationship with Sir Pitt**: Rupture complete; between Sir Pitt and whole county. Lodge-gates had not opened since Pitt's visit after marriage. Though shunned "horrid old dotard," kept strict knowledge of all happening at Hall. **Upon Sir Pitt's illness and death (Chapter 18)**: Immediately summoned; assumes command of everything; watches old Baronet through night; never seems to want sleep; does not close fiery black eyes once though Doctor snores. Calls Horrocks "tipsy old wretch"; bids him never show face again or be transported. Seizes candle; orders Mrs. Brown to search Horrocks' room; assumes authority; orchestrates household during crisis. **Post-death**: Dismissed Briggs as quickly as decency permitted; exercises dowager's authority without Mr. Pitt's objection (he thought himself injured by aunt's uncalled-for generosity to faithful retainer).

**Miss Briggs (Chapter 19)**
- **Background**: Miss Crawley's faithful retainer for score of years; received little annuity from Miss Crawley's legacy; would have been content to remain in Crawley family with Lady Jane (who was good to her and everybody). **Dismissal (Chapter 19)**: Lady Southdown dismissed her as quickly as decency permitted; Mr. Pitt made no objection (thought himself injured by aunt's generosity). **Post-dismissal (Chapter 19)**: Fatigued from weary walk to Times Office in City to insert advertisement for sixth time; reached Mr. Bowls's door where she lodged. **Reunion with Rebecca (Chapter 19)**: Rebecca recognizes her; pulls up carriage and ponies; embraces her warmly; they retire to Mrs. Bowls's front parlour with red moreen curtains and round looking-glass with chained eagle. Briggs cried; Becky laughed and kissed her. Briggs told all her history amidst uncalled-for sobs and ejaculations of wonder; women begin crying when meeting after quarrel. Rebecca gave narrative of own life with usual artlessness and candour.

**Horrocks (Butler) (Chapter 18)**
- **Sir Pitt's illness and death**: Attends evening carousing with Sir Pitt; drinks extraordinary quantity of rum-and-water; conducts master to bedroom at very late hour. **Upon Sir Pitt's collapse**: Makes wild efforts to assert authority. Called "tipsy old wretch" by Mrs. Bute; bidden never show face again or be transported "like his abominable daughter." Terrified by her manner, slunk to oak parlour. **Post-death (Chapter 18)**: Obtains small freehold from Sir Pitt's property, giving him vote for borough. Eventually becomes landlord of Crawley Arms; becomes partially reconciled with Rector of late, who occasionally steps into parlour to taste "Mr. Horrocks' mild beer."

**Bowls and Firkin (Chapter 19)**
- Received legacies from Miss Crawley and their dismissals; married and set up lodging-house according to custom of their kind. Miss Briggs lodges at Mrs. Bowls's residence with front parlour having red moreen curtains and round looking-glass with chained eagle.

**Other Characters Status Unchanged**: Colonel Dobbin, Amelia Osborne, Georgy, Lord Steyne, Lady Jane Crawley (now Lady Pitt), Reverend Bute Crawley, James Crawley, Miss Horrocks (now married to saddler at Mudbury), Hester (maid).

## Critical Facts
- **Sir Pitt dies summer 1816**: Following sudden illness after heavy drinking; becomes helpless; dies after days of decline.
- **Pitt becomes Sir Pitt, Baronet and MP**: Inherits title, Parliament seat, prospect of honours. Plans to clear estate; within days determines to rule justly, depose Lady Southdown, reconcile with blood relations.
- **Rebecca's ambitions (Chapter 18)**: Plans for Rawdon to receive Parliament seat, Court presentation for herself, secure place for husband through Lord Steyne's influence.
- **Briggs dismissed (Chapter 19)**: Released by Lady Southdown despite Miss Crawley's annuity bequest; lodges with Bowls; seeking employment through Times Office advertisements; reconnects with Rebecca, who treats her warmly.
- **Rebecca's manipulation**: Controls husband through derision of his tenderness; instructs him to spread news of inheritance; continues social climbing through Pitt's elevation and Lord Steyne's patronage.
